title: Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Link Format
summary: This RFC defines a link format for constrained web servers to describe hosted resources and their attributes and relationships. It is based on the HTTP Link header, is carried as a payload with its own media type, and uses a well-known URI for discovery.

plainLanguage.summary: Small devices on a network, such as sensors and light controllers, need to tell other devices what they can do. This document defines a short list format for that, and a fixed web address where the list lives, so that a client only has to fetch one known address to discover everything a device offers.

questions: how to discover resources on a coap server
what do rt and if mean in coap links
what is the sz attribute in link format
subtitle: A compact list format that lets tiny web servers tell clients what resources they host and how to use them.

tldr.problem: Machine-to-machine clients talking to constrained devices have no human to tell them which resources a server hosts, and fixed, hard-wired interfaces are fragile.
tldr.mechanism: Servers publish a list of links in a compact format based on the HTTP Link header, served at the well-known path /.well-known/core. Each link can carry attributes such as rt, if and sz, and clients can filter the list with a query string.
tldr.outcome: A client can GET one known URI and learn what a server offers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 6690 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the link format used for CoRE Resource Discovery, alongside the well-known URI registry entry for core and the application/link-format media type.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Constrained RESTful Environments realize the Representational State Transfer (REST) architecture in a suitable form for the most constrained nodes, for example 8-bit microcontrollers with limited memory, and networks such as IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks. CoRE is aimed at Machine-to-Machine applications such as smart energy and building automation.

The discovery of resources hosted by a constrained server is very important in machine-to-machine applications where there are no humans in the loop and static interfaces result in fragility. The discovery of resources provided by an HTTP web server is typically called Web Discovery, and the description of relations between resources is called Web Linking. In this specification, the discovery of resources hosted by a constrained web server, their attributes, and other resource relations is called CoRE Resource Discovery.

The main function of such a discovery mechanism is to provide Universal Resource Identifiers for the resources hosted by the server, complemented by attributes about those resources and possible further link relations. In CoRE this collection of links is carried as a resource of its own, as opposed to HTTP headers delivered with a specific resource. This document specifies a link format for CoRE Resource Discovery by extending the HTTP Link Header format to describe these link descriptions. The CoRE Link Format is carried as a payload and is assigned an Internet media type. A well-known relative URI /.well-known/core is defined as a default entry point for requesting the list of links about resources hosted by a server. The specification is applicable with the Constrained Application Protocol, with HTTP, or with any other suitable web transfer protocol, and the link format can also be saved in file format.

Technically, the CoRE Link Format is a serialization of a typed link as specified in Web Linking. In this specification, Web Linking is extended with specific constrained machine-to-machine attributes; links are carried as a message payload rather than in an HTTP Link Header field, and a default interface is defined to discover resources hosted by a server. This specification also defines a new relation type hosts, from the verb to host, which indicates that the resource is hosted by the server from which the link document was requested.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is that a sensor cannot tell a person what it offers, so the two devices have to work it out for themselves. A list of addresses, published at one address that everyone knows, solves that. The list reuses the format of the HTTP Link header, so it needs no special parser and stays small enough for a tiny device to produce.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
Typical use cases for Web Linking on today's web include describing the author of a web page or describing relations between web pages, such as next chapter and previous chapter. Web Linking can also be applied to machine-to-machine applications, where typed links are used to assist a machine client in finding and understanding how to use resources on a server. The document assumes that different deployments or application domains will define the appropriate REST Interface Descriptions along with Resource Types to make discovery meaningful.

In machine-to-machine applications, for example home or building automation, there is a need for local clients and servers to find and interact with each other without human intervention. The CoRE Link Format can be used by servers in such environments to enable Resource Discovery of the resources hosted by the server.

Resource Discovery can be performed either unicast or multicast. When a server's IP address is already known, either a priori or resolved via the Domain Name System, unicast discovery is performed to locate the entry point to the resource of interest. This is performed using a GET to /.well-known/core on the server, which returns a payload in the CoRE Link Format. The client then matches the appropriate Resource Type, Interface Description and possible media type for its application. These attributes may also be included in the query string in order to filter the number of links returned in a response.

Multicast Resource Discovery is useful when a client needs to locate a resource within a limited scope and that scope supports IP multicast. A GET request to the appropriate multicast address is made for /.well-known/core. To limit the number and size of responses, a query string is recommended with the known attributes. Typically, a resource would be discovered based on its Resource Type and/or Interface Description, along with possible application-specific attributes.

RESTful designs of machine-to-machine interfaces often make use of collections of resources, for example an index of temperature sensors on a data collection node or a list of alarms on a home security controller. The CoRE Link Format makes it possible to find the entry point to a collection and traverse its members; the entry point of a collection is always included in /.well-known/core to enable its discovery.

In many deployment scenarios, for example constrained networks with sleeping servers or large deployments with bandwidth limited access networks, it makes sense to deploy resource directory entities that store links to resources stored on other servers, which the document describes as a limited search engine for constrained resources. A server can register resources with a resource directory by POSTing them to /.well-known/core on the directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names three uses. Plain discovery: a client asks one server what it has. Collection discovery: a server publishes one address for a group of resources and another address listing the members. And a directory: a separate service holds the addresses for many servers, so a client can ask one place instead of scanning the network.

sections.title: The Link Format
sections.content:
The CoRE Link Format extends the HTTP Link Header field specified in Web Linking. The format does not require special XML or binary parsing, is fairly compact, and is extensible, all important characteristics for CoRE. It should be noted that this link format is just one serialization of typed links; others include HTML links, Atom feed links, or HTTP Link Header fields. It is expected that resources discovered in the CoRE Link Format may also be made available in alternative formats on the greater Internet, and the CoRE Link Format is only expected to be supported in constrained networks and machine-to-machine systems.

Section 5 of the Web Linking specification did not require an Internet media type for the defined link format, as it was defined to be carried in an HTTP header. This specification therefore defines the Internet media type application/link-format for the CoRE Link Format. Whereas the HTTP Link Header field depends on the HTTP specification for its encoding, the CoRE Link Format is encoded as UTF-8. A decoder of the format is not expected to validate the UTF-8 encoding, but is not prohibited from doing so, and does not need to perform any UTF-8 normalization. UTF-8 data can be compared bitwise, which allows values to contain UTF-8 data without any added complexity for constrained nodes.

Each link conveys one target URI as a URI-reference inside angle brackets. The context URI of a link, also called the base URI, is set to the anchor parameter when specified, otherwise to the origin of the target URI when specified, otherwise to the origin of the link format resource's base URI. Multiple link descriptions are separated by commas; commas can also occur in quoted strings and URIs but do not end a description. To convert an HTTP Link Header field to this link format, the Link: header is removed, any linear whitespace is removed, the header value is converted to UTF-8, and any percent-encodings are decoded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry looks like a target address in angle brackets, followed by a semicolon and a list of parameters such as the resource type or the interface. The text is UTF-8 and needs no special parsing. When no anchor is given, the server that served the list is assumed to be the context, which is what makes the default relation work.

sections.title: The CoRE Link Attributes
sections.content:
Three CoRE-specific target attributes are defined in addition to those already defined in Web Linking. They describe information useful in accessing the target link of the relation and, in some cases, can use the syntactic form of a URI. Such a URI may be dereferenced, for instance to obtain a description of the link relation, but that is not part of the protocol and MUST NOT be done automatically on link evaluation. When the values of attributes are compared, they must be compared as strings.

The Resource Type rt attribute is an opaque string used to assign an application-specific semantic type to a resource, which one can think of as a noun describing the resource. For a temperature resource this could be an application-specific semantic type such as outdoor-temperature, or a URI referencing a specific concept in an ontology. Multiple Resource Types may be included in the value of this parameter, each separated by a space, similar to the relation attribute. The Resource Type attribute is not meant to be used to assign a human-readable name to a resource; the title attribute is meant for that purpose. The Resource Type attribute MUST NOT appear more than once in a link.

The Interface Description if attribute is an opaque string used to provide a name or URI indicating a specific interface definition used to interact with the target resource, which one can think of as describing verbs usable on a resource. It is expected that an Interface Description will be reused by different Resource Types: the Resource Types outdoor-temperature, dew-point and rel-humidity could all be accessible using the Interface Description http://www.example.org/myapp.wadl#sensor. Multiple Interface Descriptions may be included in the value of this parameter, each separated by a space. The Interface Description attribute MUST NOT appear more than once in a link.

The maximum size estimate attribute sz gives an indication of the maximum size of the resource representation returned by performing a GET on the target URI. For links to CoAP resources, this attribute is not expected to be included for small resources that can comfortably be carried in a single Maximum Transmission Unit, but SHOULD be included for resources larger than that. There is no defined upper limit to the value of the sz attribute, and implementations must be prepared to accept large values. One implementation strategy is to convert any value larger than a reasonable size limit for the implementation to a special value Big.
sections.plainLanguage: Three attributes carry the useful information. rt says what the resource is, in the vocabulary of the application. if says how to talk to it, and can be shared by several kinds of resource. sz gives an upper bound on the size of the answer, so a client knows whether it can take the whole thing in one go.

sections.title: The Well-Known Interface
sections.content:
Resource discovery in CoRE is accomplished through the use of a well-known resource URI that returns a list of links about resources hosted by that server and other link relations. Well-known resources have a path component that begins with /.well-known/. This specification defines a new well-known resource for CoRE Resource Discovery: /.well-known/core.

A server implementing this specification MUST support this resource on the default port appropriate for the protocol for the purpose of resource discovery. It is up to the application which links are included and how they are organized. The resource is meant to return links to the entry points of resource interfaces on a server. More sophisticated link organization can be achieved by including links to CoRE Link Format resources located elsewhere on the server, for example to achieve an index. In the absence of any links, a zero-length payload is returned. The resource representation of this resource MUST be the CoRE Link Format.

The interface supports a GET on /.well-known/core to the default port, which returns the set of links available from the server. Filtering may be performed on any of the link format attributes using a query string. For example, GET /.well-known/core?rt=temperature-c would request resources with the Resource Type temperature-c. A server is not, however, required to support filtering. More capable servers such as proxies could support a resource directory by requesting the resource descriptions of other end points, or by allowing servers to POST requests to /.well-known/core; that functionality is out of scope here.

A server MAY recognize the query part of a resource discovery URI as a filter on the resources to be returned. The search name is either href, a link-param name defined in the specification, or any other link-extension name, and the value is either a complete value string that does not end in an asterisk, or a prefix value string followed by an asterisk. Value strings are percent-decoded before matching, and after those steps a complete value string matches a target attribute if it is bitwise identical, while a prefix value string matches if it is a bitwise prefix. Relation-type target attributes can contain multiple values, and each value must be treated as a separate target attribute when matching. It is not expected that very constrained nodes support filtering; implementations that do not support it must simply ignore the query string and return the whole resource for unicast requests. When using a transfer protocol that supports multicast requests, special care needs to be taken: a multicast request with a query string SHOULD NOT be responded to if filtering is not supported or if the filter does not match, to avoid a needless response storm.
sections.plainLanguage: Every server must answer a GET at /.well-known/core with its list, even if the list is empty. A client can narrow the request with a query string, for example asking only for links whose resource type is temperature-c. Servers are not required to honour filters, and a server that ignores the filter must return the whole list. On a multicast request with a filter, the server should stay silent rather than answer every caller at once.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Multiple resource descriptions in a representation are separated by commas. The examples use CoAP response codes, and are applicable to HTTP as well, where the corresponding response code would be 200 OK. A first example includes links to two different sensors sharing the same Interface Description. The default relation type for this link format is hosts in links with no rel= target attribute, so the links tell that the origin server from which /.well-known/core was requested hosts the resources /sensors/temp and /sensors/light.

A second example arranges link descriptions hierarchically, with the entry point including a link to a sub-resource containing links about the sensors. A GET of /.well-known/core returns </sensors>;ct=40, and a GET of /sensors returns </sensors/temp>;rt="temperature-c";if="sensor" and </sensors/light>;rt="light-lux";if="sensor".

An example query filter looks like a GET of /.well-known/core?rt=light-lux, which returns the single matching link. Relation-type attributes like rt, if and rel can have multiple values separated by spaces, and a query filter parameter can match any one of those values, so a resource with rt="light-lux core.sen-light" still matches a filter for rt=light-lux.

Another example shows the use of an anchor attribute to relate the temperature sensor resource to an external description and to an alternative URI. A client interested in relations about a particular resource can query on the anchor parameter, for example GET /.well-known/core?anchor=/sensors/temp.

The last example shows a large firmware resource with a size attribute. The consumer of this link would use the sz attribute to determine if the resource representation is too large and whether block transfer would be required. A client with only 64 KiB of flash might support only a 16-bit integer for storing the sz attribute, so a special flag or value should be used to indicate Big, larger than 64 KiB.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a server listing two sensors, then a server whose list points at a second address that lists the sensors in more detail. They also show filtering, and a case where a sensor has an external web page that describes it, linked with an anchor. The last example is a firmware file with a size attribute, so a small client can tell in advance that it will need to fetch the file in pieces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification has the same security considerations as described in Section 7 of the Web Linking specification. The /.well-known/core resource MAY be protected, for example using Datagram Transport Layer Security when hosted on a CoAP server.

Some servers might provide resource discovery services to a mix of clients that are trusted to different levels. For example, a lighting control system might allow any client to read state variables, but only certain clients to write state. Servers that have authentication and authorization features SHOULD support the authentication features of the underlying transport protocols and allow servers to return different lists of links based on a client's identity and authorization. While such servers might not return all links to all requesters, not providing the link does not by itself control access to the relevant resource, because a bad actor could know or guess the right URIs. Servers can also lie about the resources available. If it is important for a client to only get information from a known source, then that source needs to be authenticated.

Multicast requests using CoAP for the well-known link-format resources could be used to perform denial of service on a constrained network. A multicast request SHOULD only be accepted if the request is sufficiently authenticated and secured, for example using IPsec or an appropriate object security mechanism.

CoRE Link Format parsers should be aware that a link description may be cyclical, that is, it may contain a link to itself. These cyclical links could be direct or indirect, through referenced link resources. Care should be taken when parsing link descriptions and accessing cyclical links.
sections.plainLanguage: Hiding a resource by leaving it out of the list does not protect it, because the address can still be guessed. The list can be protected with the transport's own security, for example DTLS or TLS. A multicast request should only be answered if the requester is authenticated, since otherwise anyone can make every device on the network answer at once. And a parser has to watch out for a list that refers back to itself, directly or through another list.

viz.caption: The core of the link format grammar, as given in RFC 6690

data.title: CoRE Link Format ABNF
data.code:
Link            = link-value-list
link-value-list = [ link-value *[ "," link-value ]]
link-value     = "<" URI-Reference ">" *( ";" link-param )
link-param     = ( ( "rel" "=" relation-types )
               / ( "anchor" "=" DQUOTE URI-Reference DQUOTE )
               / ( "rev" "=" relation-types )
               / ( "hreflang" "=" Language-Tag )
               / ( "media" "=" ( MediaDesc
                      / ( DQUOTE MediaDesc DQUOTE ) ) )
               / ( "title" "=" quoted-string )
               / ( "title*" "=" ext-value )
               / ( "type" "=" ( media-type / quoted-mt ) )
               / ( "rt" "=" relation-types )
               / ( "if" "=" relation-types )
               / ( "sz" "=" cardinal )
               / ( link-extension ) )

viz.caption: The three attributes the CoRE link format adds

cells: The application-specific semantic type of a resource, like a noun for it.
The interface definition for talking to the target resource, like its verbs. It can be shared by several resource types.
The maximum size of the representation a GET on the target URI will return.
